lead: An engine instrument answers two questions from the cockpit: how fast is the engine turning, and how hot is its exhaust? A tachometer turns shaft speed into a voltage or a pulse frequency. An exhaust gas temperature (EGT) system turns exhaust heat into a small thermocouple voltage. Both signals are conditioned and shown as a number or a needle. Pilots use them at start, take-off and cruise to stay inside engine limits, and maintenance uses them to spot drift before a fault becomes a failure.
prereq: You need basic electrical measurement: voltage, current, frequency, and the millivolt as a small voltage; see 3.1 for aircraft supply and 3.13 for the other engine indicators.

blocks.text: Engine speed is measured in revolutions per minute (rpm), but the cockpit usually shows a percentage. N1 is the speed of the fan or low-pressure spool. N2 is the speed of the core or high-pressure spool. 100% is a reference speed picked by the engine manufacturer; it is not the same rpm on every engine.

A mechanical tachometer uses a flexible drive shaft from the engine gearbox to the indicator. The indicator is a small generator or a drag-cup mechanism. This is direct and needs no power, but the long shaft adds friction, lag and a path for oil leaks.

A DC tacho-generator is a small generator driven by the engine shaft. Its output voltage rises with speed: V_tacho = k × rpm. k is the generator constant in volts per rpm. The voltage is easy to measure, but brushes and commutator wear.

A magnetic or variable-reluctance pickup is better for modern engines. A coil sits close to a toothed wheel on the shaft. Each tooth changes the magnetic reluctance and induces one pulse. The indicator counts frequency, so there is no contact and no brush wear.

blocks.where: f is pulse frequency in hertz (pulses per second); rpm is shaft speed in revolutions per minute; N is the number of teeth on the wheel.

sections.h3: Exhaust gas temperature: heat becomes millivolts

blocks.text: An exhaust gas temperature (EGT) system uses a thermocouple. Two wires of different metals are joined at the hot junction, which sits in the exhaust. The other ends form the cold junction at the indicator or in a compensating circuit. A temperature difference between the junctions produces a small emf, called the Seebeck voltage. Type K uses chromel and alumel and has a sensitivity S of about 41 microvolt per degree Celsius.

blocks.where: V_TC is thermocouple voltage (µV); S is sensitivity (about 41 µV/°C for type K); T_hot is hot-junction temperature (°C); T_cold is cold-junction temperature (°C).

blocks.text: The equation shows why the cold junction cannot be ignored: the sensor reports a difference, not an absolute temperature. Cold-junction compensation adds a voltage equal to S × T_cold, or holds the cold junction at a known temperature. The compensated signal goes to a high-gain amplifier, then to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) or a moving-coil meter. An amplifier with gain G gives V_out = G × V_TC.

The display shows EGT. Some engines call the same turbine measurement TGT, turbine gas temperature. Piston engines often show cylinder head temperature (CHT), which is a different place and a different limit.

Three readings matter. At start, EGT rises to a peak and then falls as the engine stabilises. A hot start crosses the start limit; the crew shuts down. At take-off, EGT and N1/N2 are read together. On a hot day the EGT limit may be reached before the thrust target, so the limit sets take-off power. In cruise, a slow EGT drift at the same N1 can show a dirty compressor or a drifting sensor.

Do not mix N1 and N2. N1 is the fan or LP spool; N2 is the core or HP spool. Their 100% references are different speeds. A reading of 90% N2 is not 90% of N1, and it is not 90% of any universal rpm. To turn percent into rpm, use the reference speed in the engine manual.

The tachometer and EGT chains are separate until the display. A failed pickup usually gives no pulse or a noisy frequency; a failed thermocouple gives an open circuit or a fixed low reading. The cockpit may show both on one engine display, but the sensors, wires and conditioning are separate. Other engine indications are covered in 3.13; see Unit 4, Avionics Architecture, Displays and Data Buses, for digital display and data buses.

figure.caption: The top chain turns shaft speed into a voltage or frequency; the bottom chain turns exhaust heat into millivolts. Both signals are conditioned and meet at one cockpit indicator.

spec.title: Two sensor chains reaching one cockpit display
spec.aria: A shaft-driven tacho generator sends a speed signal and an exhaust thermocouple sends a millivolt signal through an amplifier, both ending at the cockpit indicator.

examples.question: A magnetic pickup faces a gear with 30 teeth on the HP shaft of a turbofan. The indicator reads 9000 rpm. (a) Find the pulse frequency in hertz. (b) A type K thermocouple with sensitivity 41 microvolt per degree Celsius has its hot junction at 700 °C and its cold junction at 25 °C. The amplifier gain is 100. Find the voltage reaching the converter in volts.
steps: Convert rpm to revolutions per second: 9000 ÷ 60 = 150 rev/s.
One pulse per tooth per revolution, so f = 150 × 30 = 4500 pulses/s = 4500 Hz.
examples.answer: (a) 4500 pulses per second (4500 Hz). (b) 2.7675 V reaches the converter.
examples.check:
rpm = 9000
teeth = 30
f = (rpm / 60) * teeth
print(f'{f:.1f}')
S = 41.0
Th = 700.0
Tc = 25.0
G = 100.0
V_uV = S * (Th - Tc)
V_mV = V_uV / 1000.0
V_out_mV = V_mV * G
V_out_V = V_out_mV / 1000.0
print(f'{V_out_V:.4f}')

traps: Using T_hot alone in V = S × T_hot instead of the difference T_hot − T_cold.
Treating N1 and N2 percentages as the same rpm; each has its own 100% reference.
Forgetting the ÷60 in f = (rpm ÷ 60) × N, or using revolutions per minute directly as hertz.
Sliding a decimal when changing microvolts to millivolts to volts; 41 µV/°C over hundreds of degrees is still only millivolts before amplification.
Assuming the cold junction is always at 0 °C; in an aircraft it sits near the instrument or in a compensating circuit and must be compensated.

quiz.q: What do N1 and N2 measure?
quiz.a: N1 is fan or low-pressure spool speed; N2 is core or high-pressure spool speed; both are usually shown as percent of a reference speed.

quiz.q: Why does a thermocouple reading depend on the cold junction?
quiz.a: It produces an emf from the temperature difference between hot and cold junctions; if the cold junction changes, the same hot temperature gives a different voltage, so compensation is needed.

quiz.q: A pickup faces a 24-tooth wheel on a shaft turning at 6000 rpm. Find the pulse frequency.
The cold junction of an EGT thermocouple is warmed from 20 °C to 50 °C while the exhaust stays at 650 °C. What happens to the uncompensated reading?
quiz.a: The difference falls from 630 °C to 600 °C; the uncompensated voltage falls by 41 × 30 = 1230 µV, so the display reads low; compensation should correct it.

quiz.q: Which two metals are used in a type K thermocouple?
A type K thermocouple has S = 41 µV/°C, hot junction 650 °C, cold junction 30 °C, and amplifier gain 50. Find the amplifier output.
Why can two engines show 90% N2 but different rpm?
quiz.a: The 100% reference is set by the manufacturer and can differ between engine types; percent is normalised, not an absolute rpm.

quiz.q: What is the difference between EGT and CHT?
quiz.a: EGT is exhaust gas temperature near the exhaust or turbine; CHT is cylinder head temperature on a piston engine; they use different sensors and limits.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engine displays combine N1, N2, EGT, fuel flow and vibration into one engine-indicating and crew-alerting system, and the raw sensors feed digital buses. Research moves toward thin-film thermocouples and fibre-optic temperature sensors for faster response and immunity to electromagnetic interference. Search for 'cold junction compensation', 'variable reluctance speed sensor' and 'engine indicating and crew alerting system' to go further.
